items.passage: Online resale was supposed to be a simple matter of matching unused goods with buyers, and in one respect it worked: transaction costs fell far enough that items once thrown away became worth listing. The environmental accounting turned out to be less simple. A garment sold secondhand stays in use longer, which displaces some new production, but the platform also increases the total number of garments in circulation by making it easy to buy cheaply and resell quickly. Studies of the effect have found modest net reductions in emissions, smaller than the platforms' own estimates, largely because the displaced purchase is often not a new garment but another used one.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the environmental benefit of resale depends on
choices: whether a secondhand purchase replaces a new purchase or another used one
how many items a platform lists in a year
whether the platform charges a commission
the fiber content of the garments being sold
choice_notes: correct
listing volume is not the mechanism described
fees are not discussed
fiber content is not mentioned
items.explanation: The emissions reduction comes from displacing new production, so the benefit shrinks when the displaced purchase would have been secondhand anyway.
items.skill_note: Find the substitution the benefit depends on.

items.passage: Online resale was supposed to be a simple matter of matching unused goods with buyers, and in one respect it worked: transaction costs fell far enough that items once thrown away became worth listing. The environmental accounting turned out to be less simple. A garment sold secondhand stays in use longer, which displaces some new production, but the platform also increases the total number of garments in circulation by making it easy to buy cheaply and resell quickly. Studies of the effect have found modest net reductions in emissions, smaller than the platforms' own estimates, largely because the displaced purchase is often not a new garment but another used one.
items.stem: Which finding would most directly support the passage's explanation for the modest emissions reductions?
choices: Surveys of resale buyers found that most of their purchases replaced items they would otherwise have bought used.
Resale platforms reported record numbers of listings in each of the past five years.
The average garment is worn fewer times than it was two decades ago.
Secondhand clothing is cheaper per item than new clothing.
choice_notes: correct
listing growth shows scale, not substitution
this describes declining utilization without linking it to resale
price difference is the premise, not the explanation
items.explanation: The passage attributes the small reduction to secondhand purchases displacing other secondhand purchases. Evidence that most buyers would otherwise have bought used shows exactly that substitution pattern.
items.skill_note: The right evidence measures the mechanism, not the market's size.

items.passage: The technique of memory palaces is old enough to be attributed to a poet who supposedly recalled the guests at a banquet by picturing them in the order they had sat. The method works by converting a list into a route: you place each item in a familiar location and later walk the route in imagination, retrieving items as you pass them. Its effectiveness depends on spatial memory, which is unusually durable, and on the fact that locations provide an order that the items themselves lack. Modern experiments have found that trained participants can recall long lists with few errors, though the advantage fades when the material is abstract and the locations are not distinctive.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the method would be least effective for
choices: a list of unrelated abstract terms placed in identical rooms
a shopping list placed along a familiar walking route
a speech organized around rooms in the speaker's home
a list of names placed in a childhood neighborhood
choice_notes: correct
this matches the conditions the passage describes as favorable
a familiar route supports the method
a familiar route supports the method
items.explanation: The passage says the advantage fades when material is abstract and locations are not distinctive. Identical rooms are the extreme case of indistinct locations.
items.skill_note: For a "least effective" inference, invert both favorable conditions at once.

items.passage: In swing-era dance bands, the rhythm section kept time for the dancers, and its patterns were steady enough to step to. Bebop changed the job. Playing for listeners in small clubs rather than dancers in ballrooms, drummers moved the pulse from the bass drum to the ride cymbal and began dropping accents in unexpected places; pianists stopped comping in regular chords and inserted sparse, syncopated figures; bassists played walking lines that outlined harmony rather than marking beats. The result was a texture in which the time was implied rather than announced. Dancers found it hard to follow, which was, for some of its makers, part of the point.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the shift described in the passage was connected to
choices: a change in the audience and setting for the music
a decline in the number of drummers
new recording technology that hid the bass drum
a shortage of dance halls in large cities
choice_notes: correct
the number of drummers is not discussed
recording is not mentioned
no shortage is described
items.explanation: The passage explicitly contrasts dancers in ballrooms with listeners in small clubs, and then says dancers found the new texture hard to follow, which ties the musical change to its new setting.
items.skill_note: When a passage names a setting before describing a change, the setting is part of the explanation.

items.passage: A translator of poetry works under a constraint that is easy to state and hard to satisfy: the version must be a poem in the new language and a faithful rendering of the old one, and the two requirements pull against each other. Fidelity to meter may require a different word; fidelity to the word may break the meter. Translators resolve the conflict differently, and their choices are legible in the result: one version preserves the rhyme and alters the images, another keeps the images and abandons the rhyme. Neither is a failure. What would be a failure is a version that claims to have preserved everything, since the claim would mean the translator had stopped noticing the losses.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Poetry translation requires visible trade-offs, and a claim to have preserved everything is itself a kind of failure.
Poetry should not be translated because the losses are too great.
Rhyme is more important than imagery in translation.
Translators agree on a single best method for rendering meter.
choice_notes: correct
the passage says neither approach is a failure
the passage presents the two goals as competing, not ranked
the passage says translators resolve the conflict differently
items.explanation: The passage frames translation as a conflict between two legitimate demands, shows that different resolutions are defensible, and singles out only the denial of loss as a failure.
items.skill_note: The concession "neither is a failure" narrows the main idea to the final claim.

items.stem: The final sentence suggests that the author regards a claim of complete preservation as
choices: evidence that the translator is no longer attending to what was lost
the mark of an unusually skilled translator
the only honest position for a translator to take
a technical impossibility that no translator has considered
choice_notes: correct
the passage calls such a claim a failure
the passage treats the claim as self-deceiving
the claim is presented as a temptation, not an impossibility
items.explanation: The author reasons that the claim could only be made by someone who had stopped noticing losses, which makes the claim a symptom of inattention.
items.skill_note: "Since the claim would mean" introduces the author's diagnosis of the claimer.

items.passage: Restoring a color film from the 1930s is not a matter of returning it to a state it once had. The dyes in early color stock faded unevenly, so a print that has aged has a color balance no audience ever saw, but neither did any audience see the camera negative, which was never projected. Restorers work from multiple sources, negatives, separations, surviving prints, and make judgments about which artifacts are damage and which are the record of a process. A restored film is therefore a reconstruction with an argument behind it, and the argument is visible: two restorations of the same title can differ in warmth, in contrast, and in what they choose to leave unretouched.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author would describe a "definitive" restoration as
choices: unattainable, because restoration requires interpretive choices among sources
achievable if the camera negative survives
the standard that most restorers now meet
necessary before a film can be screened
choice_notes: correct
the negative was never projected, so it does not define the audience's view
the passage says restorations differ
screening is not discussed
items.explanation: If every restoration is a reconstruction with an argument, no version can be definitive, because the choices could have been made differently.
items.skill_note: Inferences about labels often hinge on the passage's claim that a single original does not exist.

items.passage: The claim that recording froze jazz is a strange one, given that the music was improvised and that the records are the main reason anyone can hear it now. What the claim gets at is a distinction between a performance and a document. Before recording, a solo existed only in the room where it was played and in the memory of those who heard it; a musician could play the same piece differently every night, and often did. Recording made one of those nights into a text. Later musicians learned solos from records, note for note, and the practice of transcription gave the music a repertoire of fixed statements that it had not previously had. Whether that is a loss depends on whether you think a tradition is best carried in memory or in notation.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author's attitude toward the "frozen jazz" claim is
choices: that it names a real change but mischaracterizes it as a loss
that it is entirely correct and needs no qualification
that it is baseless and should be dismissed
that it applies only to musicians who could not read music
choice_notes: correct
the passage calls the claim strange and reframes it
the passage takes the distinction seriously rather than dismissing it
music literacy is not discussed
items.explanation: The author grants the underlying observation, that performance became document, but treats "frozen" as a misdescription, since the final sentence leaves the value question open rather than settled.
items.skill_note: Look for the sentence where the author translates the claim into something more precise.

items.passage: The light had to be trimmed before dark, and Kettlewell would not let her do it alone until she could name every part of the lamp without looking. So she stood on the iron stair with the wick in her hand while he counted, and when she reached the top she found that the fog had come in below them, a gray floor where the harbor had been. The bell was already sounding. She thought, with a calm that surprised her, that the ships out there were steering by a light she could put out with two fingers, and that her father had done this every night for nineteen years without once mentioning what it weighed.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the narrator's calm comes from
choices: a newly felt understanding of responsibility
confidence that the fog will lift before morning
relief that her father has stopped counting
certainty that no ships are near the harbor
choice_notes: correct
no forecast is given
the counting is part of the instruction, not a source of relief
the bell and the fog imply the opposite
items.explanation: The calm arrives with the realization that ships depend on a light she controls, which replaces fear with a sense of consequence.
items.skill_note: Note where the emotion is placed relative to the realization.

items.passage: She worked at the kitchen table after the house was quiet, the dictionary on one side and the manuscript on the other, and the sentence she could not solve was a single line in which a woman crosses a courtyard at dusk. The problem was the verb. It meant to walk without purpose, but it carried a suggestion of pleasure that the English "wander" did not, and "stroll" was too leisured, and "drift" made her sound like smoke. At two in the morning she wrote "went out into the courtyard, unhurried," and sat looking at it, aware that she had explained something the original had merely done.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: A translator settles on a phrase that is accurate but more explicit than the original's single verb.
A translator decides that the original sentence cannot be translated at all.
A writer is revising a novel about a woman in a courtyard.
The dictionary provides a precise equivalent for the verb.
choice_notes: correct
she produces a version, though an imperfect one
the scene describes translation, not composition
the dictionary fails her, which is why she improvises
items.explanation: The passage follows a failed search for an equivalent and ends with a solution the translator recognizes as more explanatory than the original.
items.skill_note: The final clause carries the main idea in this kind of passage.

items.passage: She worked at the kitchen table after the house was quiet, the dictionary on one side and the manuscript on the other, and the sentence she could not solve was a single line in which a woman crosses a courtyard at dusk. The problem was the verb. It meant to walk without purpose, but it carried a suggestion of pleasure that the English "wander" did not, and "stroll" was too leisured, and "drift" made her sound like smoke. At two in the morning she wrote "went out into the courtyard, unhurried," and sat looking at it, aware that she had explained something the original had merely done.
items.stem: The final clause suggests that the translator feels her solution
choices: clarifies a quality the original conveyed implicitly
improves on the original's meaning
preserves the original's ambiguity exactly
fails because it uses two words instead of one
choice_notes: correct
she notices the difference with unease, not triumph
the clause says she explained what the original merely did
the solution is more explicit, not equally ambiguous
items.explanation: "Explained something the original had merely done" contrasts explicit statement with enacted quality, which is exactly the loss she registers.
items.skill_note: Distinguish "more explicit" from "better" or "equivalent."

items.passage: Carnegie funded more than 2,500 libraries, but he rarely chose their books. The design was standardised: a small reading room, a closed stack, and a librarian's desk positioned to see the door. What varied was the collection, assembled locally by women's clubs and school boards. Historians who study these buildings now argue that the standardised architecture mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the historians mentioned in the text believe that
choices: whether a town obtained a library depended more on local organisers than on the standardised building plan
Carnegie's architects designed each library to suit the town that received it
the size of a library's collection was determined by its building's design
women's clubs and school boards preferred standardised buildings to varied ones
choice_notes: correct
contradicted by 'the design was standardised'
contradicted by 'what varied was the collection'
never claimed; their role was assembling collections
items.explanation: The historians argue the architecture 'mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all' — so local organising, not the plan, determined who got a library.
items.skill_note: Inference answers are paraphrases of a causal claim already in the text.

items.passage: The idea that forest trees share resources through fungal threads has become one of ecology's most popular stories. The evidence is real but narrower than the story. In experiments, labeled carbon applied to one tree does appear in neighboring seedlings, and fungal hyphae do connect roots. What is disputed is the direction and the meaning: whether the transfer is a tree-to-tree donation, a fungus moving carbon for its own purposes, or a byproduct of roots and fungi trading locally. A recent review that re-examined the field's strongest claims found that many rested on experiments unable to distinguish among these possibilities. The network exists; the generosity attributed to it does not yet.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the claim that trees deliberately transfer carbon to struggling neighbors through fungal networks?
choices: Fungal threads connect trees of the same species more often than trees of different species.
Most of the carbon moving through fungal threads was consumed by the fungus rather than deposited in neighboring trees.
Fungal networks are more extensive in old-growth forests than in recently planted stands.
Trees in the same stand often share several species of fungal partner.
choice_notes: relatedness patterns do not address whether transfer is directed
correct
this describes where networks are dense, not why carbon moves
shared partners are consistent with the claim rather than damaging to it
items.explanation: The claim requires carbon to reach the neighbor as a benefit. If the fungus absorbs the carbon for itself, the transfer is fungal nutrition rather than tree-to-tree donation, which is the alternative the passage raises. The other findings concern network distribution or partner overlap and leave the direction of benefit untouched.
items.skill_note: A weakening finding must attack the mechanism the claim depends on, not a surrounding fact.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Recording turned performances into fixed texts, a change whose value depends on how one thinks a tradition should be carried.
Recording destroyed jazz by making improvisation impossible.
Transcription is a marginal practice with little influence on jazz.
Jazz musicians before recording played the same solos every night.
choice_notes: correct
the passage says the claim is "strange" and reframes rather than endorses it
the passage credits transcription with giving the music fixed statements
the passage says musicians often played pieces differently
items.explanation: The passage moves from skepticism about the frozen-jazz claim to a narrower distinction between performance and document, and it closes by making the verdict depend on a view about tradition. A preserves that neutrality.
items.skill_note: When a passage ends by relativizing a judgment, the main idea must not take a side.

items.rule: Its is possessive; it's means it is.
items.passage: The company announced ______ new headquarters would open in the spring, nearly a year later than planned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: its
it's
its'
it is
choice_notes: correct
expands to 'it is', which does not fit
no apostrophe is used for a possessive pronoun
expands to 'it is', which does not fit
items.explanation: The sentence needs a possessive pronoun modifying 'headquarters': 'its'. 'It's' and 'it is' would each mean 'it is new headquarters', and possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, so 'its'' is not a word.
items.skill_note: Test the expansion: if 'it is' fits, use it's; otherwise use its.

items.rule: A nonessential phrase set off by an opening comma must be closed by a comma before the main verb.
items.passage: The report on the city's water quality, which had been commissioned after several complaints from residents ______ that lead levels had fallen sharply since 2019.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: residents, concluded
residents concluded
residents; concluded
residents: concluded
choice_notes: correct
leaves the nonessential phrase unclosed
semicolons cannot separate a subject from its verb
a colon cannot separate a subject from its verb
items.explanation: The phrase 'which had been commissioned after several complaints from residents' is nonessential, so it must be enclosed by commas on both sides. Only the first choice supplies the closing comma before the main verb 'concluded'. A semicolon or colon between a subject and its verb is never correct.
items.skill_note: Check that both sides of a nonessential phrase are closed.

items.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with a noun inside a prepositional phrase.
items.passage: The collection of letters and photographs donated by three generations of the family ______ now housed in the county archive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: is
are
were
have been
choice_notes: correct
agrees with 'letters and photographs' instead of 'collection'
plural and past tense
plural
items.explanation: The subject is 'The collection', which is singular; 'of letters and photographs donated by three generations of the family' only modifies it. The singular present 'is' is the only choice that agrees.
items.skill_note: Cross out every prepositional phrase between subject and verb, then check agreement.

items.rule: Items joined by 'and' in a series must share the same grammatical form.
items.passage: The internship teaches students how to draft a budget, how to present findings to a client, and ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: how to negotiate a deadline
negotiating deadlines
to negotiating a deadline
deadline negotiation
choice_notes: correct
breaks the pattern of 'how to' plus verb
unidiomatic and unparallel
a noun phrase where the other items are verb phrases
items.explanation: The first two items are 'how to draft' and 'how to present', so the third must also be 'how to' plus a verb: 'how to negotiate a deadline'. Parallel structure in a list is decided by the form of the first item.
items.skill_note: Match the third item to the first, not to the one nearest it.

items.rule: An introductory participial phrase must modify the subject of the main clause.
items.passage: Walking through the exhibition for the first time, ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the visitors were struck by the size of the canvases
the size of the canvases struck the visitors
the canvases' size was striking to visitors
it struck the visitors how large the canvases were
choice_notes: correct
the size did not walk through the exhibition
the canvases' size did not walk through the exhibition
an expletive subject leaves the modifier unattached
items.explanation: 'Walking through the exhibition' must describe whoever is doing the walking. Only the first choice makes 'the visitors' the subject, so only it attaches the modifier correctly.
items.skill_note: Ask who is doing the action in the opening phrase, then make that the subject.

items.rule: Use the past perfect for an action completed before another past action.
items.passage: By the time the survey was published in 1998, the volunteers ______ more than two thousand hours of observations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: had logged
have logged
will have logged
log
choice_notes: correct
present perfect does not fit a completed past sequence
future perfect contradicts 'was published'
present tense contradicts the past frame
items.explanation: The logging happened before the 1998 publication, and both events are in the past, so the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'had logged'.
items.skill_note: Two past actions in sequence: the earlier one gets 'had'.
